issue_title: The Rising Cost of Living in Nevada: Health Care

baskets.often_moved: In this dataset, similar ideas often became law or cleared both chambers
baskets.unfinished: Majority floor votes, both-chamber passage, or strong momentum without enactment
baskets.rarely_moved: Repeated early stops (especially the first committee) for this kind of idea

2019.note: one adopted study resolution (SCR10) recorded outside the bill milestone machine

theme_scorecards.label: Licensing doctors, nurses, and other providers: compacts, endorsement, scope of practice
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (22 of 41 non-enactments); the Nurse Licensure Compact specifically died in its first committee in 2021, 2023, and 2025
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: profession-by-profession compacts and endorsement bills pass with unanimous or near-unanimous floor votes; the nurse compact is the exception that never reaches a floor.

theme_scorecards.label: Where care happens: hospitals, clinics, urgent care, telehealth, rural access
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: access and telehealth bills usually become law; bills that set or cap facility prices (82:AB85, 83:AB349) die before a floor vote.

theme_scorecards.label: Medicaid and public coverage: reimbursement rates, eligibility, administration
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (11) or the origin-house floor/money stage (9)
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: narrowly-scoped Medicaid rate raises pass unanimously; systemic rate reviews and broad rate raises die at the money stage.

theme_scorecards.label: What health plans and Medicaid must cover
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: mandates split evenly; several passed one chamber unanimously and died in the second (80:SB200, 80:SB235).

theme_scorecards.label: Prescription drug costs, pharmacies, and pharmacy benefit managers
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (10); the two price-cap bills that reached the desk were vetoed (82:AB250, 83:AB259); full PBM regulation died late twice (82:SB352, 83:SB316)
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: transparency and Medicaid-side PBM bills pass; bills that cap prices or regulate PBMs across the commercial market stop late - in the second house, the amendment shuttle, or at the governor's desk.

theme_scorecards.label: Growing the provider workforce: medical education, residencies, loan repayment, recruitment money
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (8) or origin floor (7) - mostly money-stage deaths of funding and tax-credit designs
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: direct state programs (residency grants, loan repayment) become law; the tax-credit funding design died on the Senate floor twice (82:SB369, 83:SB269).

theme_scorecards.label: How insurers treat patients and providers: prior authorization, denials, networks, credentialing
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (8); three vetoes (83:SB128 AI denials, 82:AB439 forced arbitration, 83:SB352 nondiscrimination)
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: insurer-conduct bills that reach a floor pass nearly unanimously; the 2025 AI-denial ban is the one that passed both houses and was vetoed.

theme_scorecards.label: Patient bills, medical debt, price transparency, and surprise billing
theme_scorecards.typical_stop: first committee (7); vetoed at the desk when it got there (83:AB204 medical debt, 82:AB437 paperwork fees, 83:AB282 billing errors)
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: the 2019 out-of-network emergency billing law is the standout; since then, patient-cost bills have the lowest pass rate of any theme and drew three of the record's fifteen vetoes.

theme_scorecards.label: Insurance market structure: pooling, association plans, the public option, the exchange
theme_scorecards.inference: Inference: small set; the Public Option (81:SB420) is the only major enactment in the record that passed on a near party-line vote (12-9, 26-15).

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Adopt interstate licensure compacts (e.g., the Nurse Licensure Compact) to expand provider supply.
proposal_reality_cards.record: Compacts pass easily for some professions and keep dying for nurses. Enacted, all with unanimous or near-unanimous floor votes: the Physical Therapy Compact (2019 SB186; re-enacted 2025 AB248, 41-1 and 21-0), the EMS personnel compact (2023 AB158, 42-0 and 21-0), the Audiology and Speech-Language Pathology Compact (2025 AB230, 41-0 and 21-0), and licensure by endorsement for dental hygienists (2025 AB334, 42-0 and 21-0). The Nurse Licensure Compact - the compact citizens named - has been filed three times and never reached a floor vote: 2021 AB142 (a Republican sponsor team) and 2023 AB108 both died in Assembly Commerce and Labor, and in 2025 it was folded into SB34, a five-compact omnibus (PA, nurse, audiology/SLP, PT, OT) that died in Senate Commerce and Labor while the audiology/SLP and PT compacts passed as separate bills. For physicians, the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact already sits in Nevada statute from before this record's window - SB34's own digest places the PA compact 'in the same chapter as the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact' - and the record's physician measures ease individual licensure further: 2025 SB124 (foreign medical graduates' path to full licensure) passed 41-0 and 21-0, while the 2019 provisional-license design (SB259) died on the Senate floor.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: The first committee - Assembly Commerce and Labor (2021, 2023) and Senate Commerce and Labor (2025) - for the nurse compact; the omnibus packaging did not change the outcome. Early PT compact retries died in the second house after 21-0 Senate votes (2021 SB100, 2023 SB97).
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Assemblymember Elaine Marzola (D) carried the three 2025 single-profession compacts (AB106, AB230, AB248); the 2021 nurse compact came from Republicans O'Neill, Titus, and colleagues; Sen. Heidi Seevers Gansert (R) carried the PT compacts; 2023 AB108 and 2025 SB34 were committee bills.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: Fully a state-legislature lever: compacts are enacted as state statutes. The 25-year multi-state findings participants cited are not in this dataset; what the Nevada record shows is the pattern of which compacts reached a floor.
open_questions: What objection stops the nurse compact in committee while the PT, EMS, and audiology compacts pass unanimously - and is it different in Assembly versus Senate Commerce and Labor?
Would a stand-alone NLC bill fare differently than the 2025 omnibus packaging?
The physician compact is already in Nevada statute - is the licensure barrier participants described a compact gap at all, or a board-processing one?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Increase the overall supply of physicians and providers.
proposal_reality_cards.record: The largest supply bill in the record became law three months late. 2025 SB434 (Senate Majority Leader Cannizzaro) created the Statewide Health Care Access and Recruitment Grant Program - competitive grants against critical provider shortages - passed the Senate 18-2 and the Assembly 42-0 as amended, and died on the session's last day when the Senate did not concur in the Assembly amendment. The 36th (2025) Special Session then enacted the same program as SB5 (15-6 and 37-0, Chapter 12), housing it under the new Nevada Health Authority. Around it sits a steady record: Health Service Corps funding enacted in 2019 (SB289) and 2021 (SB233), dental therapy licensed in 2019 (SB366), workforce-data laws enacted in 2021 (AB278, SB379). The failures cluster at the money stage: the 2023 Health Service Corps refill (AB248) died in committee, the workforce-needs assessment (2025 SB495) passed the Senate 13-8 and died in the Assembly, and a proposed health-workforce office (2025 SB425) died on the Senate floor.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Money: committee and floor deaths concentrate in Ways and Means / Finance territory and end-of-session calendars. SB434's death was procedural (amendment concurrence), not a vote against it - no chamber ever voted it down.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Sen. Joseph Hardy (R) carried the Health Service Corps line (2019, 2021); Sen. Cannizzaro (D) carried SB434; the special-session SB5 passed with both parties' votes in the Assembly (37-0).
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: A state-legislature lever, and now an existing program: the Statewide Health Care Access and Recruitment Grant Program is in statute with an account under the Nevada Health Authority. The 'roughly 500 doctors' gap participants cited is not measured in this dataset.
open_questions: The grant program is now law - is the next question its funding level rather than a new bill?
What did the Assembly's Amendment 972 change in SB434, and does SB5 as enacted reflect it?
Does the new Nevada Health Authority placement change who decides where grants go?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Fund more graduate medical education / residency programs.
proposal_reality_cards.record: A state residency-grant program is already in statute: 2023 SB350 created grants for new and expanded physician residency programs (passed 21-0 and 40-0) and 2025 SB262 revised it (21-0 and 42-0) - both carried by Sen. Julie Pazina (D) with co-sponsors from both parties' orbit. What keeps failing is the funding design that runs through tax credits: Sen. Robin Titus's (R) bills giving businesses credits for donations to residency programs died on the Senate floor in 2023 (SB369) and 2025 (SB269), and the 2019 direct appropriation for postgraduate residencies (AB311, Krasner R) died in its first committee. The pathway bills pass: 2025 SB124 (Doñate D) eased foreign medical graduates' path to full licensure, 41-0 and 21-0. The combined debt-plus-residency design (2023 AB393, Kasama R + Lange D) died in its first committee, and 2025 AB170's associate-physician licenses died the same way.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: The money stage: tax-credit versions died on the origin floor (where revenue bills go to wait), and appropriations versions died in first committees. The grant-program design that passed went through the standard policy committees with committee-of-the-whole support.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Sen. Julie Pazina (D) carried the enacted grant program twice; Sen. Robin Titus (R) carried the tax-credit design twice; Sen. Fabian Doñate (D) carried the foreign-graduate pathway.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: A state-legislature lever with a program already on the books; residency slots also depend on federal Medicare GME funding, which no Nevada bill controls - the state bills fund state grants on top.
open_questions: SB350/SB262 grants exist - what has the program funded so far, and is the constraint appropriations rather than statute?
Why does the tax-credit funding design die on the Senate floor when the same goal passes as a grant program?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Offer student-loan / medical-debt forgiveness for providers serving in-state or in rural areas.
proposal_reality_cards.record: Participants described this as not yet drafted; the record shows it is Nevada's most consistently enacted recruitment tool. The Nevada Health Service Corps - loan repayment for providers who commit to underserved areas - was funded in 2019 (SB289, 41-0 and 21-0) and 2021 (SB233, 42-0 and 19-0), both carried by Sen. Joseph Hardy (R). 2023 AB45 created a broader program repaying student loans of health providers working in underserved communities (41-0 and 21-0). In 2025 the Legislature expanded eligibility twice: AB269 added speech-language pathologists, physical therapists and others (40-2 and 21-0), and SB266 widened qualifying provider types again (42-0 and 21-0). The failures are the bigger-money versions: the 2019 stand-alone loan-repayment program (AB358, Republican sponsors) died on the origin floor, the 2021 physician-stipend design (AB372, Kasama R) died in committee, the 2023 Health Service Corps refill (AB248) died in committee, and the behavioral-health expansion (AB69) died on the origin floor in 2023.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Nothing stops the policy; money stops the scale. Every failure died at a committee or floor money stage, never on a recorded floor vote against it.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Sen. Joseph Hardy (R) built the Health Service Corps funding line; the 2025 expansions came from Assemblymember Reuben D'Silva (D) and Sens. Angela Taylor and Michelee Cruz-Crawford (D). Republican sponsor teams carried the failed larger designs (AB358, AB372, AB248).
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: A state-legislature lever with the machinery already in statute; the rural-funding tie-in participants floated (federal rural money as the source) does not appear in any bill in this record.
open_questions: The programs exist - what are their current appropriations and how many providers do they actually place?
Would a service-commitment design tied to medical debt (not just student loans) require a new statute or an amendment to the existing programs?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Reform / limit insurance prior authorization (including AI-driven denials).
proposal_reality_cards.record: 2025 was the breakthrough-and-veto year. What passed: AB463 (Backus D) tightened prior-authorization rules and deadlines for private insurers, Medicaid, and the Children's Health Insurance Program - 42-0 and 20-0, now law. What was vetoed: SB128 (Neal D), barring insurers from relying solely on artificial intelligence to deny prior-authorization requests - the AI-denial concern participants raised - passed the Assembly 23-16 and the Senate 15-6 and was vetoed. AB290 (Nguyen D), the bill participants named as having died and being planned for reintroduction, cleared Assembly Commerce and Labor with amendments, was re-referred, and died without further action at session's end; three other 2025 prior-auth bills (AB295, AB470, SB398 - two of them Republican-led) died in their first committees. The earlier record: all three 2019 attempts died in committee (AB225, AB372, SB359), while the adjacent step-therapy limits passed unanimously in 2023 (SB167, SB194) and dental-denial review by a dentist passed in 2025 (AB202, 42-0 and 20-0).
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Historically the first committee (all of 2019's bills; three of 2025's). In 2025 the live chokepoint moved to the governor's desk for the AI piece: SB128 is one of the record's fifteen vetoes.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: 2025 bills came from both parties: Backus (D, enacted AB463), Nguyen (D, AB290), Yurek and Edgeworth (R, AB295), Kasama (R, AB470), Rogich (R) with Ohrenschall (D) on SB398; Sen. Dina Neal (D) carried the vetoed AI ban.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: State law reaches state-regulated plans, Medicaid, and CHIP - AB463 covers exactly that set. The record does not show what the SB128 veto objected to (no veto messages in this dataset).
open_questions: AB463 is new law - which of AB290's provisions did it absorb, and what remains for a refile?
What would the AI-denial ban need to change to survive the desk, and does its 23-16 Assembly margin leave room for an override strategy?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Reduce administrative burden and eliminate insurance middlemen, including pharmacy benefit managers.
proposal_reality_cards.record: The transparency layer is law; the regulation layer keeps dying within sight of the finish. Enacted: 2019 AB141 (Republican-carried) barred PBMs from gagging pharmacists who tell patients about cheaper options; 2019 SB276 ordered the drug-cost and rebate study; 2019 SB378 made Medicaid drug contractors pass rebates back to the state; 2023 AB434 protected 340B providers from PBM penalties; and 2025 SB389 (Scheible D + Stone R) put Medicaid prescription drugs under a single state-contracted PBM, 41-0 and 18-2. The failures escalate in reach and die later: licensing PBMs under the state health department died in committee in 2021 (SB392); making PBMs follow the same rules as the insurers they serve passed the Senate 21-0 in 2023 (SB352, Scheible D + Buck R) and died in the Assembly; the 2025 rewrite SB316 (Nguyen D + Stone R + Titus R) passed the Senate 18-2 and the Assembly 42-0 and died on the final day without concurrence; and the two committee-stage retries (SB149, SB209) died in 2025. No bill in this record proposes eliminating middlemen outright - every design regulates, licenses, or consolidates them.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Two different walls: first committees for licensing designs (2021 SB392, 2023 AB440, 2025 SB149/SB209) and the end-of-session amendment shuttle for the broad rewrites (2023 SB352 died in the second house after 21-0; 2025 SB316 died awaiting concurrence after 42-0 and 18-2). No PBM-regulation bill has ever lost a floor vote in this record.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Consistently cross-party: Melissa Hardy and Roberts (R) on AB141; Scheible (D) with Buck (R) on SB352 and with Stone (R) on SB389; Nguyen (D) with Stone and Titus (R) on SB316. Sen. Jeff Stone (R) appears on four PBM bills.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: State law reaches PBMs serving state-regulated plans and Medicaid; the enacted 2025 design consolidates Medicaid pharmacy middlemen into one audited contract rather than removing the function.
open_questions: SB316 passed both houses and died on the calendar - is a clean refile the shortest path, and what did the final amendments change?
Does the single-PBM Medicaid contract (SB389) produce the savings its design assumes - and does that model extend to commercial plans?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Improve provider-network accuracy and speed up insurance credentialing.
proposal_reality_cards.record: This is the thinnest record of the ten proposals. What exists: 2019 SB234 requires insurers to use a standardized letter and report trends when they reject a provider's application to join a network - passed 21-0 and 39-0, the one direct network-admission law in the set. 2023 SB494 funded Medicaid's computer systems including centralized provider credentialing (enacted, 20-0 and 42-0) - an administrative modernization, not a mandate on insurers. No bill in this record sets credentialing deadlines for insurers, audits network-directory accuracy, or defines 'full' panels. The adjacent attempts died: 2019 SB290 (Hardy R, network plans paying out-of-network providers for unanticipated care) died in its first committee, and 2021 SB90 (Hardy R, keeping unfounded investigations from counting against providers in credentialing) passed the Senate 21-0 and died in the Assembly.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Not enough attempts to name a pattern; the two failures split between a first committee and the second house. Certainty: low - single-example patterns are insufficient for strong conclusions.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Sen. Joseph Hardy (R) carried both failed adjacent bills; the enacted pieces were committee bills.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: Split lever: state law can regulate credentialing of state-licensed plans (SB234 shows the form); network contracts and panel-size decisions are otherwise private contracting, and Medicaid credentialing runs through the state's own systems (SB494).
open_questions: A credentialing-deadline or directory-accuracy mandate has never been filed - what would its committee path be, Commerce and Labor or Health and Human Services?
Did SB234's rejection-letter and trend-reporting data ever get analyzed, and does it show the 'full panel' pattern participants described?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Expand insurance pooling for small businesses and non-employer groups.
proposal_reality_cards.record: Nevada has legislated in this space in every direction except the one participants sketched. 2019 SB481 set state rules for association health plans and self-funded multiple-employer arrangements offering small-business coverage (passed 21-0 and 39-0). 2021 SB396 let public agencies pool with private entities to purchase prescription drugs and medical supplies (21-0 and 40-1). The biggest structure is the Public Option: 2021 SB420 (Cannizzaro D) created a state-designed plan any Nevadan can buy - the record's rare contested enactment, 12-9 in the Senate and 26-15 in the Assembly. A 2019 study resolution (SCR10) on a public health-coverage plan was adopted. What died: the 2019 state bulk drug-purchasing list (SB226, Spearman D) in its first committee. No bill in this record creates an any-group pooling mechanism - the association/credit-union design participants floated has never been filed.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Too few failures to name one; the enacted bills moved through Health and Human Services committees. The Public Option's 12-9 / 26-15 vote is the closest thing in this record to a party-divided outcome on market structure.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Committee bills carried the association-plan rules; Sen. Cannizzaro (D) carried the Public Option; Sen. Spearman (D) carried purchasing-pool designs.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: Partly a state lever: the record's bills regulate state-licensed association plans and state purchasing. The employer-based structure participants called the key obstacle is federal tax and benefits law; no state bill in this record can or does repeal it.
open_questions: The Public Option exists in statute - what is its implementation status, and does it serve the small-business buyers participants described?
Would an any-group pool be regulated under SB481's association-plan framework, or need a new one?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Increase insurance reimbursement rates to attract and retain providers.
proposal_reality_cards.record: The record splits cleanly by scope. Targeted Medicaid raises become law, usually unanimously: autism behavior-technician rates to at least $52/hour (2021 SB96), letting provider-assessment money fund higher Medicaid payments to more provider types (2023 SB435, after the Assembly version AB197 died on the origin floor), special billing categories and rates for children's cancer clinics (2023 SB221) and mental-health training clinics (2025 SB353), family-caregiver payment (2025 SB185, 41-1 and 21-0), epilepsy-device rates (2025 AB284), and dropping the out-of-state cap on autism rates (2025 SB497). Systemic reform dies at the money stage: the 2019 study of paying Medicaid rates that reflect actual provider costs (AB116) died on the origin floor, the 2023 rate-review overhaul (AB99) died the same way, across-the-board children's rate raises died in committee twice (2023 SB255 and 2025 SB239, both Buck R), the 2025 substance-use rate raise (SB150) and the mental-health rate resolution (SB366, Krasner R) died in committee, and the payment-rate study (2021 AB347) died on the floor. On the commercial side, vision-plan contract-and-reimbursement rules passed twice (2021 AB436, 2025 AB448 - Koenig R). The backdrop: the 31st (2020) Special Session's budget bill AB3 cut FY2020-2021 appropriations including Department of Health and Human Services budgets (passed 36-6 and 21-0).
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: The money committees and the origin-house floor: every broad rate bill died before reaching the second chamber. No broad rate raise has ever received a floor vote in this record.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Both parties carry rate bills: Buck (R) twice on children's rates, Krasner (R) on the federal-rate resolution, Ohrenschall and Dondero Loop (D) on autism rates, Brown-May (D) on the rate-review overhaul, Koenig (R) on vision reimbursement.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: Split lever: the Legislature sets Medicaid rates through the budget; commercial reimbursement is contractual, and the record's commercial bills regulate contract terms (vision plans) rather than setting rates. Medicare and Tricare rates - the examples participants used - are federal and appear in no Nevada bill.
open_questions: Is the binding constraint statute or the biennial budget - and would the 2019 AB116-style cost study change the budget conversation?
The provider-assessment mechanism (2023 SB435) funds rate raises without General Fund money - which provider types could it extend to?

proposal_reality_cards.citizen_statement: Right-size the care setting (urgent care vs. ER) and use rotating/staffed clinics for access.
proposal_reality_cards.record: The split-billing model participants designed - separating ER from urgent care so minor issues don't incur ER charges, with rotating physicians or a state-paid physician per county - has never been filed in this record. What exists around its edges: the 2019 out-of-network emergency billing law (AB469, 38-3 and 21-0) limits what out-of-network providers can bill patients for emergency care; 2023 SB497 adjusted the arbitration system for those payment disputes; 2019 AB317 made off-campus hospital sites offering urgent care or emergency care carry distinct provider identifiers; and 2023 AB277 (Koenig R) let small 24/7 rural emergency hospitals operate in Nevada, 41-0 and 21-0. The bills that tried to control what emergency facilities charge died early: 2023 AB85 (Orentlicher D, a state process to set hospital and emergency-center prices) died on the origin floor, and 2025 AB349 (Orentlicher D, capping charges for public-employee plans at Medicare multiples) died in its first committee. Telehealth - the other access lever participants debated - is largely settled law: 2021 SB5 modernized coverage, 2023 SB119 kept payment parity, and 2023 AB276 extended it to provider-to-provider consultation.
proposal_reality_cards.chokepoint: Facility price-control bills die early (origin floor 2023, first committee 2025); facility access bills pass unanimously. The delivery-model redesign has no chokepoint because it has no bill.
proposal_reality_cards.who_carried: Assemblymember David Orentlicher (D) carried both price-control attempts; Gregory Koenig (R) carried the rural emergency hospitals law; telehealth bills were mostly committee-sponsored.
proposal_reality_cards.venue_note: Mixed lever: Nevada licenses facility types (AB277 shows the form) and regulates billing of state-regulated plans, but ER billing practice also runs through federal Medicare rules - 2019 AB232 (requiring most hospitals to join Medicare, obligating emergency care regardless of ability to pay) is where the record touches that layer. County-level staffed clinics would be a county budget question no bill in this record addresses.
open_questions: Would the split-billing model be a facility-licensing bill (like AB277) or an insurance-billing bill (like AB469) - and which committee owns each?
The price-control versions died twice under one sponsor - is the design or the scope (all payers vs. public employees) what stopped them?
What does the state-paid-county-physician idea cost, and has any interim committee ever scoped it?

people_and_process_signals.committee_choke_points: Of the 95 policy bills that died in their first committee: Senate Health and Human Services 22, Assembly Commerce and Labor 21, Senate Commerce and Labor 19, Assembly Health and Human Services 16, money committees 10, other committees 7.
people_and_process_signals.veto_pattern: All 15 policy vetoes fall in 2023 (8) and 2025 (7), concentrated on patient-cost and insurer-conduct bills: drug price caps tied to Medicare maximums (82:AB250, 83:AB259), medical-debt collection limits (83:AB204), billing-error response duties (83:AB282), the AI prior-authorization ban (83:SB128), forced-arbitration ban (82:AB439, after 42-0 in the Assembly), provider-employment limits for hospitals (82:AB11), nurse staffing committees (83:SB182), Medicaid managed-care profit reinvestment (82:SB400), gender-affirming-care license protections (82:SB302, 83:SB171), insurance nondiscrimination (83:SB352), pharmacy language access (82:AB251), and paperwork-fee limits (82:AB437).

deliberation_prompts: The nurse compact died in its first committee three times while four other professions' compacts passed unanimously. What is different about nursing's committee audience, and what would change it?

SB434 and SB316 both passed both houses in 2025 and died in the end-of-session amendment shuttle; one was revived in the special session, the other was not. What decides which finish-line deaths get a second chance?
Loan repayment for underserved-area providers is already in statute and keeps expanding. Is the gap here a new program, or the size of the appropriation?

Prior-authorization deadlines are now law (AB463) while the AI-denial ban was vetoed (SB128). Does the veto pattern hit only bills that constrain insurer decision tools, and what does that mean for a refile?

Every broad Medicaid rate reform died at the money stage while narrow rate raises passed unanimously. Is scope the price of passage - and does that path ever add up to the systemic raise participants want?
The record's fifteen vetoes all fall in 2023-2025 and cluster on patient-cost bills. Which of the ten proposals are exposed to that pattern, and which historically escape it?
Cross-party sponsor teams appear on 54 policy bills and 36 became law. Which of the ten proposals could plausibly attract one, judging by who has already carried adjacent bills?

The network-accuracy and credentialing proposal has essentially no legislative record. Is that because the lever is regulatory (Division of Insurance) rather than statutory - and has anyone checked what SB234's reporting data shows?

The ER-versus-urgent-care model has never been filed. Would a facility-licensing design (like the rural emergency hospital law) or an insurance-billing design (like the 2019 surprise-billing law) fit it better?
data_limits_carried_forward: The set is broad (keyword + full subject-index harvest) but not a proven complete universe.
The record shows where bills stopped, never why - no veto messages or floor debate in this dataset.
Committee Yea votes are partly inferred (membership minus recorded Nay/Absent) and marked in the source data.
Party labels: 97.7% of roll-call ballot rows matched to official NELIS rosters; sponsor party coverage is 100% (three names resolved from NELIS legislator pages).
Special-session facts (31st AB3, 36th SB5) come from a manual verification file, not the regular pipeline.
